```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(must)
has_emmeans <- requireNamespace("emmeans", quietly = TRUE)
```

Calling a combined effect additive, synergistic or antagonistic is a
statement about a null model, not about the data alone. must separates the
three decisions behind such a statement and makes each one visible in the
output:

1. **What the design can identify** (`describe_design()`): which treatment
   combinations exist, which interactions they identify, which cells are
   shared, how the experimental units were replicated and sampled, and
   whether some stressor was applied to whole groups of units.
2. **Which model fits the data** (`fit_responses()`): a generalised linear
   mixed model per response, with its error distribution chosen for the
   data and not for the null model.
3. **What "non-additive" means** (`estimate_interactions()`): each
   combination of stressors is tested against one or more null models, each
   on its own scale, with the same criteria and from the predictions of the
   same model (Madge Pimentel et al. 2025), with a correction for
   experiments with few replicates. Simple addition (AD) is the default (see
   "The default null model"); multiplication (MU) and dominance (DO), the
   other null models of Madge Pimentel et al. (2025), Bliss independence
   (BL), with the emergent three-way interaction of Beppler et al. (2016),
   the stress addition model (SAM) of Liess et al. (2016) and concentration
   addition (CA, Loewe additivity) are chosen in `null_models`, by name or
   with `suggest_null_models()`, which applies the guidelines of Schäfer &
   Piggott (2018) to what is known about the stressors. The same tests apply
   to a model fitted with another package (see "Models fitted outside
   must").

`report_interactions()` then writes the methods of the analysis and the
table of every decision behind it, from the settings of the objects.

## A worked example: insecticide, herbicide and nutrients

`polazzo_zooplankton` comes from an outdoor mesocosm experiment with a full
factorial of chlorpyrifos, diuron and nutrient enrichment, three mesocosms
per combination (Polazzo & Rico 2021). Zooplankton were sampled five days
before the pesticide application and on days 7, 14, 30 and 50 after it.
Because nutrient additions started four weeks before the pesticides, day -5
is not a pre-treatment baseline for all stressors; the example uses the four
samplings after the application. Besides the design, the table has the total
density and one column per taxon; the first eight columns are the design and
the three responses analysed below.

```{r data}
zoo <- polazzo_zooplankton[polazzo_zooplankton$day > 0, ]
head(zoo[, 1:8])
```

### 1. The design

```{r example-design}
design <- describe_design(
  zoo,
  stressors = c("insecticide", "herbicide", "nutrients"),
  control = c(insecticide = "absent", herbicide = "absent", nutrients = "ambient"),
  unit = "mesocosm",
  time = "day"
)
design
design$sets[, c("set_id", "stressors", "net_identifiable", "pure_identifiable", "shared")]
```

The full factorial identifies the three pairwise interactions and both the
net deviation and the pure interaction of the three stressors. All four sets
share the control, and the mesocosms are measured repeatedly.

### 2. One model per response

Each response gets the candidates that suit its values (here positive
densities, with zeros for *Daphnia*); the one selected is the one with the
lowest AIC among those that converge and, by default, pass the DHARMa
residual checks. The checks are switched off here only because the vignette
must build without DHARMa.

```{r example-fit}
fits <- fit_responses(zoo, c("total_density", "cyclopoida", "daphnia"), design,
                      residual_checks = FALSE, seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
fits
fits$fits$total_density$selection[, c("family", "link", "converged", "aic", "selected")]
fits$fits$daphnia$reason
```

*Daphnia* was absent from every mesocosm of some treatment combinations on
some days. With a log link their means lie on the boundary of the parameter
space, where intervals from the model are not valid, so they are fixed there.
When such a combination is the one a contrast compares with its reference
(the herbicide alone against the control, say), the contrast is tested from
the probability of observing only zeros if the null model held
(`status = "boundary"`); when it is a cell the null model needs to compute
its expectation, the contrast is `not_estimable`.

### 3. Which null models?

`suggest_null_models()` applies the guidelines of Schäfer & Piggott (2018,
Fig. 3) to what is known about the stressors. Chlorpyrifos inhibits an enzyme
of the nervous system, diuron the photosynthesis of algae, and the nutrients
add resources: the three stressors do not act similarly, and the insecticide
acts specifically on physiology. The effect is a change in density, not
mortality, and with one level of each stressor the experiment gives no
stressor-effect relationship. How the sensitivities of the taxa to the
stressors are correlated is not known, nor is the distribution of their
sensitivities, so both are left unknown (`NA`, the default). The effects of
each stressor alone, as shares of the effect limit (here the loss of the
whole density), are estimated from the models in every contrast set and on
every day, without using the combinations of stressors.

```{r example-suggest}
choice <- suggest_null_models(fits, similar_action = FALSE, specific_action = TRUE,
                              mortality = FALSE, stressor_effect = FALSE)
choice
table(choice$sets$response, choice$sets$type, useNA = "ifany")
```

The unknown correlation of the sensitivities keeps dominance (if it were
highly positive) besides simple addition and the multiplicative model, and in
most sets and days the effects are too uncertain to tell whether their sum
exceeds the effect limit, which would call for the multiplicative model.

Stressors need not reduce a response. With three mesocosms per treatment most
single effects cannot be told from zero (`"double neutral"`), but the
insecticide increases the total density on day 7 and the cyclopoid copepods on
day 50, and the nutrients increase *Daphnia* on days 14 and 30 (`"positive
neutral"`, the types of Piggott et al. 2015); the cells of *Daphnia* with only
zeros give no interval, so their direction is not known (`NA`). The guidelines
take such effects with their sign: an increase offsets the decreases in the
sum of the effects, which exceeds the effect limit when simple addition would
predict a density below zero, and it rules out concentration addition and the
stress addition model, which assume effects in one direction and stressors
that reduce the response. For a proportion such as survival that the
stressors alone increase, the guidelines are applied to its complement, and
`estimate_interactions()` then needs the `sensitivity` that the suggestion
gives. The guidelines were written for individuals and populations; for a
community total, Schäfer & Piggott (2018) point to the compositional null
model of Thompson et al. (2018), which predicts it from the null models of
each taxon. `choice$sets` gives the null models reached in each set and day.

### 4. Null models

The guidelines leave the three null models of Madge Pimentel et al. (2025).
`estimate_interactions()` takes them from `choice` and keeps its criteria and
reasons in `settings$null_model_choice`:

```{r example-estimate}
est <- estimate_interactions(fits, null_models = choice, n_sim = 4000, seed = 2021)
e <- est$estimates
triple <- e[e$response == "total_density" & e$order == 3L & e$component == "interaction" &
              e$null_model != "DO",
            c("time", "null_model", "estimand", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "df",
              "p_value", "p_adjusted", "status")]
triple
```

On day 7 the net deviation of the three stressors is negative under AD and
MU, while the pure three-way interaction is not: the deviation is carried by
the pairwise interactions, which the full factorial lets us estimate. After
the adjustment for the many sets and times tested, neither is significant
with 24 mesocosms. The rows with `time = "overall"` average each effect over
the four samplings.

```{r example-pairs}
pairs7 <- e[e$response == "total_density" & e$time == "7" & e$order == 2L &
              e$component == "interaction" & e$null_model != "DO",
            c("stressors", "null_model", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "p_adjusted")]
pairs7
summary(est)
```

### 5. Classes

```{r example-classify}
cls <- classify_interactions(est)
table(cls$class, cls$order, useNA = "ifany")
cls[cls$response == "total_density" & cls$time == "7" & cls$null_model == "AD",
    c("stressors", "pattern", "class", "borderline")]
```

With the correction for small samples and the adjustment for multiple tests,
no interaction of this experiment deviates clearly from the null models.

```{r example-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
plot(est, response = "total_density", null_model = "MU")
```

### 6. Methods and decisions

`report_interactions()` writes the statistical methods of this analysis from
the settings of `est` and, if given, of the classes and of the comparison of
null models: the design, the model selected for each response and how, the
null models and the criteria behind them, and how the interactions were
estimated and tested, with the works cited. Every value comes from the
objects, so the text matches the analysis that was run; the description of
the experiment itself (organisms, exposure, measurements) is left to the
authors.

```{r example-report}
report <- report_interactions(est, classes = cls)
cat(report$methods, sep = "\n\n")
```

The table of decisions gives, for every argument, the value used, its
default and its source: the default, set by the user, chosen by must (the
distribution selected, a seed drawn at random), estimated (criteria of the
guidelines evaluated from the effects), taken from `suggest_null_models()` or
recorded (versions). The decisions that differ from the defaults are those a
reviewer will look for first:

```{r example-decisions}
changed <- !report$decisions$source %in% c("default", "recorded")
report$decisions[changed, c("decision", "value", "source")]
```

`print(report)` shows the paragraphs, the table and the references as plain
text. In an R Markdown or Quarto document, a chunk with `results = "asis"`
and `cat(format(report, format = "markdown"), sep = "\n")` inserts them as
paragraphs, a table and a list of references. A justification of the null
models can be added with `justification`.

## Additive, or only not detected?

A non-significant interaction is a failure to detect a deviation: with few
replicates most interactions are classed "AD" whatever their true size. To
claim that a combination follows a null model, declare before the analysis
the largest deviation that would be negligible, as a share of the response of
the reference cell, in `margin`. Each interaction is then also tested for
equivalence, with two one-sided tests (Schuirmann 1987; Lakens et al. 2018),
on its relative deviation, (observed − expected) / reference, which is on the
same scale for every null model. Each test measures how many standard errors
separate the estimated means from the closest means at which the deviation
equals the margin, on a scale on which the variance of a mean does not
depend on the mean (the square root for counts, for example), so it does not
depend on `inference`.

In ten tanks per combination where copepods follow the multiplicative model
exactly:

```{r equivalence}
tanks <- expand.grid(salinity = c("ambient", "high"), warming = c("no", "yes"),
                     replicate = 1:10, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
tanks$tank <- seq_len(nrow(tanks))
mu <- 100 * ifelse(tanks$salinity == "high", 0.7, 1) * ifelse(tanks$warming == "yes", 0.8, 1)
tanks$copepods <- qpois((tanks$replicate - 0.5) / 10, mu)
tank_design <- describe_design(tanks, c("salinity", "warming"),
  control = c(salinity = "ambient", warming = "no"), unit = "tank")
tank_fit <- fit_responses(tanks, "copepods", tank_design, residual_checks = FALSE,
                          seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
eq <- estimate_interactions(tank_fit, null_models = c("AD", "MU"), n_sim = 4000, seed = 1,
                            margin = 0.1)
eq$estimates[eq$estimates$component == "interaction",
             c("null_model", "relative", "relative_lower", "relative_upper", "p_adjusted",
               "p_equivalence_adjusted")]
classify_interactions(eq)[, c("null_model", "class", "verdict")]
```

Both null models give the class AD, but only the multiplicative one is
equivalent within ±10% of the control. Under simple addition no deviation is
detected, but it could be larger than the margin: the verdict is
inconclusive. A deviation detected but within the margin would be
`"negligible"`. With three mesocosms per combination, no interaction of the
zooplankton experiment is equivalent even within ±25% of the control: they
are inconclusive, not additive.

```{r equivalence-zoo}
eq_zoo <- estimate_interactions(fits, null_models = c("AD", "MU"), n_sim = 4000, seed = 2021,
                                margin = 0.25)
table(classify_interactions(eq_zoo)$verdict, useNA = "ifany")
```

The margin has no default: which deviation is negligible depends on the
response and on the question, and has to be fixed before the results are
seen. Equivalence also needs replication: in simulated 2 x 2 experiments
with four units per combination, a margin of ±10% was never reached. The
test kept its nominal error for Gaussian responses, survival and
overdispersed counts analysed with a quasi-Poisson `glm()` or with the
negative binomial of `fit_responses()`. It declared false equivalences too
often when a Poisson model, which ignores the overdispersion, was fitted to
the same counts (21% of the experiments, instead of 5%; that is why
`fit_responses()` uses the Poisson only when the negative binomial does not
converge), and with `MASS::glm.nb()` (10%; see "Equivalence" in
`?estimate_interactions`).

## Few replicates: the small-sample correction

Madge Pimentel et al. (2025) obtain the uncertainty of the null-model
contrasts by simulating the fixed effects from a normal distribution with
their estimated covariance (Krinsky & Robb 1986). With the replication of
most mesocosm experiments that is too optimistic: the variance is estimated
by maximum likelihood, which underestimates it with few degrees of freedom,
and the normal ignores the uncertainty of that estimate. In simulated 2 x 2
experiments with three replicates per combination, the asymptotic tests
rejected a true null model in 10–17% of the cases instead of 5%. By default
(`correction = "small_sample"`) must refits the selected model by REML and
draws from a multivariate t whose degrees of freedom follow the experimental
units (column `df`). For a Gaussian model without random effects the AD
intervals of the delta method are then exactly those of `lm()`, and the
simulation approximates them:

```{r correction}
small <- data.frame(
  salinity = rep(c("ambient", "high", "ambient", "high"), each = 3),
  warming = rep(c("no", "no", "yes", "yes"), each = 3),
  growth = c(10.2, 9.1, 10.9, 8.3, 7.4, 8.8, 7.1, 6.0, 7.6, 3.2, 4.6, 3.9)
)
small$jar <- seq_len(nrow(small))
small_design <- describe_design(small, c("salinity", "warming"),
  control = c(salinity = "ambient", warming = "no"), unit = "jar")
small_fit <- fit_responses(small, "growth", small_design,
  families = list(gaussian = gaussian()), residual_checks = FALSE, seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
interaction_row <- function(x) {
  x$estimates[x$estimates$component == "interaction",
              c("estimate", "lower", "upper", "df", "p_value")]
}
rbind(
  delta = interaction_row(estimate_interactions(small_fit, null_models = "AD",
                                                inference = "delta")),
  simulation = interaction_row(estimate_interactions(small_fit, null_models = "AD",
                                                     n_sim = 20000, seed = 1)),
  asymptotic = interaction_row(estimate_interactions(small_fit, null_models = "AD",
                                                     n_sim = 20000, seed = 1,
                                                     correction = "none"))
)
reference <- lm(growth ~ salinity * warming, data = small)
confint(reference)[4, ]
summary(reference)$coefficients[4, "Pr(>|t|)"]
```

With repeated measures or subsamples the degrees of freedom are those of the
units (units minus treatment combinations), and for stressors applied to
whole groups of units, those of the groups. Poisson and binomial models
without random effects have no variance to estimate and keep the normal
distribution. `correction = "none"` gives the asymptotic procedure, for
comparison with published analyses.

## Interactions in the presence of other stressors

By default each interaction is estimated with the stressors outside the set
at control: the insecticide × herbicide interaction compares mesocosms
without added nutrients. With `background = "all"` the design also gives the
same interaction in the presence of each level of the other stressors, with
that background as the reference:

```{r background}
design_all <- describe_design(zoo, c("insecticide", "herbicide", "nutrients"),
  control = c(insecticide = "absent", herbicide = "absent", nutrients = "ambient"),
  unit = "mesocosm", time = "day", background = "all")
design_all$sets[, c("set_id", "stressors", "background")]
```

## When an increase means sensitivity

MU and DO describe mechanisms (independent action, dominance of the
strongest stressor) only when an increase in the response means tolerance:
survival rather than mortality, abundance rather than damage. For responses
measured the other way, give their names in `sensitivity`: binomial
responses (successes out of `trials`, see `fit_responses()`) are then
analysed as their complement, and for other responses MU and DO are reported
as `not_applicable`.

```{r sensitivity}
jars <- data.frame(
  copper = rep(c("no", "yes", "no", "yes"), each = 5),
  heat = rep(c("no", "no", "yes", "yes"), each = 5),
  dead = c(1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 8, 9, 10, 9, 9),
  n = 10
)
jars$jar <- seq_len(nrow(jars))
jar_design <- describe_design(jars, c("copper", "heat"),
  control = c(copper = "no", heat = "no"), unit = "jar")
jar_fit <- fit_responses(jars, "dead", jar_design, trials = c(dead = "n"),
  residual_checks = FALSE, seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
mortality <- estimate_interactions(jar_fit, null_models = c("AD", "MU", "DO"), n_sim = 4000,
                                   seed = 1, sensitivity = "dead")
mortality$estimates[mortality$estimates$component == "interaction",
                    c("null_model", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "p_value", "note")]
```

## What a design can and cannot identify

A design identifies an interaction only if it contains the control, each
stressor alone and their combination. Many experiments are not full
factorials. In a ray design, for example, two compounds are tested alone at
three doses and the mixture only at matching doses:

```{r ray}
ray <- data.frame(
  fungicide = c(0, 2, 20, 200, 0, 0, 0, 2, 20, 200),
  insecticide = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 20, 200, 2, 20, 200)
)
ray <- ray[rep(seq_len(nrow(ray)), each = 3), ]
ray$mesocosm <- seq_len(nrow(ray))
ray_design <- describe_design(
  ray,
  stressors = c("fungicide", "insecticide"),
  control = c(fungicide = "0", insecticide = "0"),
  unit = "mesocosm"
)
ray_design
ray_design$sets[, c("set_id", "levels", "net_identifiable", "shared")]
```

Only the three diagonal combinations are identifiable, and all three share
the same control: their interaction estimates are correlated, so finding the
same class at the three doses is not three independent confirmations.

### A control shared by several groups, and stressors that start later

Sometimes one control serves several `by` groups: the same two stressors
applied as pulses or as a press, in two orders, or to upstream and
downstream ponds. Copying the control into each group would count its units
twice. `shared` marks the rows that belong to every group of a `by` column;
here the control tanks (`regime = "both"`) complete the sets of both
regimes:

```{r shared}
regimes <- data.frame(
  regime = rep(c("both", "pulse", "pulse", "pulse", "press", "press", "press"), each = 4),
  heat = rep(c("no", "yes", "no", "yes", "yes", "no", "yes"), each = 4),
  pesticide = rep(c("no", "no", "yes", "yes", "no", "yes", "yes"), each = 4)
)
regimes$tank <- seq_len(nrow(regimes))
shared_design <- describe_design(
  regimes,
  stressors = c("heat", "pesticide"),
  control = c(heat = "no", pesticide = "no"),
  unit = "tank", by = "regime", shared = c(regime = "both")
)
shared_design$sets[, c("regime", "levels", "net_identifiable", "shared")]
```

The two sets use the same control, so their estimates are correlated, as in
the ray design. Without `shared`, neither regime has a control and nothing is
identifiable.

When a stressor starts later than the others (drying from day 0, after
weeks of warming), the samplings before it are pre-treatment for that
stressor only. A named list in `baseline`, such as
`baseline = list(drying = c(-36, -1))`, keeps the interactions that involve
drying from being estimated before it was applied, while those among the
other stressors are estimated at those times.

### Units inside groups: blocks, whole plots and confounding

A stressor is often applied to whole groups of units: one temperature per
climate room, one nitrate level per header tank, CO2 per plot. Then the
replication of that stressor is the number of groups, not of jars or
mesocosms. `groups` tells `describe_design()` which columns group the units.
Here temperature is applied to whole rooms and nutrients vary within them:

```{r rooms}
rooms <- expand.grid(temperature = c("15", "20"), room_rep = 1:2,
                     nutrients = c("no", "yes"), jar = 1:3, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
rooms$room <- paste0("R", rooms$temperature, "-", rooms$room_rep)
rooms$jar_id <- seq_len(nrow(rooms))
one_room <- rooms[rooms$room_rep == 1, ]
one_design <- describe_design(
  one_room,
  stressors = c("temperature", "nutrients"),
  control = c(temperature = "15", nutrients = "no"),
  unit = "jar_id", groups = "room"
)
one_design$groups[, c("group", "between", "structure", "groups_per_combination", "random")]
one_design$sets[, c("stressors", "net_identifiable", "confounded")]
```

With one room per temperature, every effect of temperature, its interaction
with nutrients included, is also a difference between two rooms: the set is
`confounded`, and its estimates and class carry that flag. A random intercept
for rooms cannot separate them (its variance is not identifiable), so none is
added. With two rooms per temperature the rooms are whole plots: temperature
effects are replicated by rooms, and `fit_responses()` adds a random
intercept for them by default.

```{r rooms-replicated}
two_design <- describe_design(
  rooms,
  stressors = c("temperature", "nutrients"),
  control = c(temperature = "15", nutrients = "no"),
  unit = "jar_id", groups = "room"
)
two_design$groups[, c("group", "between", "structure", "groups_per_combination", "random")]
```

Blocks that hold every treatment combination (`structure = "blocks"`) also
get a random intercept. The design cannot reveal groups that are not in the
data: a shared incubator or water supply must be recorded to be checked.

## Three or more stressors: net deviation and pure interaction

With three stressors, the deviation of ABC from the combination of the
single effects (the **net** deviation) includes the pairwise interactions
AB, AC and BC. The **pure** third-order interaction is what remains once
those are removed, and it needs all eight combinations. In this simulated
2 x 2 x 2 experiment the pure interaction is negative, but part of the net
deviation comes from the pairwise terms:

```{r three-way}
grid <- expand.grid(nitrate = c("ambient", "high"), sediment = c("no", "yes"),
                    flow = c("normal", "low"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
n <- grid$nitrate == "high"
s <- grid$sediment == "yes"
f <- grid$flow == "low"
grid$mean <- 20 - 3 * n - 4 * s - 2 * f + 1.5 * n * s - n * f + 0.5 * s * f -
  2.5 * n * s * f
streams <- grid[rep(seq_len(8), each = 4), ]
streams$biomass <- streams$mean * rep(c(0.95, 1.02, 0.98, 1.05), 8)
streams$channel <- seq_len(nrow(streams))
stream_design <- describe_design(
  streams,
  stressors = c("nitrate", "sediment", "flow"),
  control = c(nitrate = "ambient", sediment = "no", flow = "normal"),
  unit = "channel"
)
stream_fit <- fit_responses(streams, "biomass", stream_design,
  families = list(gaussian = gaussian()), residual_checks = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
stream_est <- estimate_interactions(stream_fit, null_models = "AD",
  inference = "delta")
int <- stream_est$estimates[stream_est$estimates$component == "interaction", ]
int[, c("stressors", "estimand", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
```

The net deviation of the triple equals its pure interaction plus the three
pairwise interactions. If the design lacked the pairwise combinations, the
pure interaction would be reported as `not_identifiable` and
`describe_design()` would warn that the net deviation cannot be split.

## Bliss independence and emergent interactions

Under Bliss independence (`null_models = "BL"`; Bliss 1939) stressors act
independently, so the responses relative to the reference cell,
w = y / y0 (relative fitness or survival), multiply. The net interaction is
wABC - wA wB wC, and the emergent interaction of Beppler et al.
(2016, eq. 2.4), wABC - wA wBC - wB wAC - wC wAB + 2 wA wB wC, is the part
of the three-way deviation that the pairwise interactions do not explain.
For the stream channels:

```{r bliss}
bliss <- estimate_interactions(stream_fit, null_models = c("MU", "BL"), n_sim = 4000,
                               seed = 1)
b <- bliss$estimates
b[b$component == "interaction" & b$order == 3L,
  c("null_model", "estimand", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "p_value", "rescaled",
    "rescaled_class")]
```

The net BL interaction tests the same hypothesis as the net MU interaction
on another scale: both have the same sign in every simulation draw, so their
simulated p-values coincide. The emergent interaction is a different
hypothesis from the pure MU interaction, which removes the pairwise
interactions on the log scale.

`rescaled` divides each BL interaction by its value at an extreme (a
combination with no response for negative interactions, one equal to the
most affected single stressor for positive ones; Segrè et al. 2005, Beppler
et al. 2016), and `rescaled_class` applies the cut-offs of Beppler et al.
(2016) at -0.5 and 0.5. Here the emergent interaction is clearly below zero
(its interval excludes zero) but small relative to lethal synergy, and the
cut-offs would call it additive. must decides from the interval and the
p-value, as for the other null models, and reports the rescaled value only
as a description of size: fixed cut-offs ignore the uncertainty of the
estimate (Madge Pimentel et al. 2025). The emergent interaction is defined
here for three stressors; with four or more it is `not_defined`.

## Stress addition and concentration addition

Two more null models come from ecotoxicology. The stress addition model
(`"SAM"`; Liess et al. 2016) assumes that each individual tolerates a
general stress drawn from a beta distribution: the effect of each stressor
alone becomes the general stress that causes it, the stresses add up, and
the predicted survival of the combination is the share of individuals that
tolerate their sum. Concentration addition (`"CA"`, Loewe additivity) treats
each stressor as a dilution of the others: a combination is additive when
the doses, each divided by the dose of that stressor alone with the same
effect, add up to one (Loewe 1953; Tang et al. 2015). CA needs the
dose-response curve of each stressor, so it needs at least two doses of each
stressor tested alone, with numeric levels; in two-level factorials it is
`not_defined`. must fits a two-parameter log-logistic curve to the responses
at those doses, relative to the control, and refits it in each simulation
draw.

In this ray design, survivors out of 20 animals per jar were generated so
that the two pesticides follow concentration addition exactly:

```{r sam-ca}
doses <- data.frame(fungicide = c(0, 5, 20, 80, 0, 0, 0, 5, 20, 80),
                    insecticide = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 4, 16, 1, 4, 16))
mixtures <- doses[rep(seq_len(nrow(doses)), each = 4), ]
mixtures$jar <- seq_len(nrow(mixtures))
mixtures$n <- 20
survival <- function(f, i) {
  if (f == 0 && i == 0) return(0.95)
  # Log-logistic curves with EC50 30 (slope 1.5) and 6 (slope 2)
  eq <- function(w) f / (30 * ((1 - w) / w)^(1 / 1.5)) + i / (6 * ((1 - w) / w)^(1 / 2)) - 1
  0.95 * uniroot(eq, c(1e-9, 1 - 1e-9))$root
}
p <- mapply(survival, mixtures$fungicide, mixtures$insecticide)
mixtures$alive <- qbinom(c(0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8)[(mixtures$jar - 1) %% 4 + 1], 20, p)
mixture_design <- describe_design(mixtures, c("fungicide", "insecticide"),
  control = c(fungicide = "0", insecticide = "0"), unit = "jar")
mixture_fit <- fit_responses(mixtures, "alive", mixture_design, trials = c(alive = "n"),
  residual_checks = FALSE, seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
mix <- estimate_interactions(mixture_fit, null_models = c("BL", "SAM", "CA"), n_sim = 4000,
                             seed = 1)
m <- mix$estimates
m[m$component == "interaction",
  c("levels", "null_model", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "p_adjusted")]
```

The same mixtures are additive under CA, show no clear deviation from Bliss
independence, and are antagonistic under SAM, which predicts much larger
combined effects than the other two. Which null model fits a pair of
stressors is a mechanistic question that the data alone cannot settle (Tang
et al. 2015; Madge Pimentel et al. 2025): name the model with each claim of
synergy or antagonism.

`compare_null_models()` sets the null models side by side:

```{r sam-ca-compare}
compare_null_models(mix)[, c("levels", "BL", "SAM", "CA", "agreement", "direction")]
```

The deviations at the two higher doses are model-dependent: only SAM flags
them. An interaction that every plausible null model flags with the same
sign (`"robust"`) does not depend on that choice; one that only some of them
flag, or that they flag in opposite directions (`"conflicting"`), needs the
mechanistic hypothesis to be interpreted. With two or more null models,
`summary()` also counts these cases.

## The default null model

When there is a hypothesis about how the stressors act, the null model that
represents it should be named in `null_models` (Madge Pimentel et al. 2025),
and `suggest_null_models()` derives the null models that the guidelines of
Schäfer & Piggott (2018) give for what is known. Without either, must uses
simple addition. That default was chosen by
simulation, with a rule fixed before the results were seen: among the null
models defined in two-level factorials and with at least 80% of the highest
average power against interactions that no mechanism explains, the one with
the fewest false interactions on average over five mechanisms of no
interaction, each with the same weight. The simulated experiments were 2 x 2
factorials and 3 x 3 dose factorials with four units per combination, with
survival out of 20 animals or overdispersed counts as the response, and
moderate or weak single effects. The data of each experiment followed one of
the five mechanisms without interaction, or a synergy (half the response
that the most harmful mechanism predicts) or an antagonism (halfway between
the most affected single stressor and the control) that none of them
explains. Each experiment was analysed with a cell-means `glm()` and
`estimate_interactions(model, design)`, and an interaction was flagged when
p < 0.05 (100 experiments per scenario).

Percentage of experiments with an interaction flagged, averaged over designs,
responses and effect sizes (CA is tested in the dose design only; for two
stressors MU and BL give the same test):

| Data generated by | AD | MU, BL | DO | SAM | CA |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AD, no interaction | 4.8 | 10.6 | 20.2 | 28.2 | 8.1 |
| MU (BL), no interaction | 6.7 | 4.9 | 12.1 | 32.5 | 9.7 |
| DO, no interaction | 19.7 | 14.8 | 3.2 | 44.5 | 25.0 |
| SAM, no interaction | 60.2 | 76.4 | 85.8 | 4.0 | 34.7 |
| CA, no interaction | 9.7 | 13.9 | 37.9 | 23.4 | 2.6 |
| *False interactions, mean* | *20.2* | *24.1* | *31.9* | *26.5* | *16.0* |
| Synergy | 79.0 | 97.4 | 99.4 | 10.8 | 51.2 |
| Antagonism | 37.6 | 36.9 | 21.6 | 64.8 | 51.8 |
| *Power, mean* | *58.3* | *67.1* | *60.5* | *37.8* | *51.5* |

Each null model flags interactions at about the nominal rate when the data
follow its own mechanism (the diagonal); elsewhere in the first five rows the
tests are not wrong: the definitions of "no interaction" disagree. No null
model was robust to every mechanism: data generated by stress addition
looked synergistic to all the others, and data generated by the others
looked antagonistic to stress addition. AD had the fewest false interactions
among the null models that two-level factorials can test. CA had fewer in
the dose design (16%, against 23% for AD there), with less power (51%
against 63%), and needs at least two doses of each stressor tested alone.
AD was also chosen within each design, each size of the single effects and
with survival as the response. Without the stress addition mechanism, MU and
BL came within one percentage point of AD and, being more powerful, would
have been chosen; with counts only, the power of AD fell below 80% of theirs,
and they would have been chosen too. Requiring every null model to agree
(`agreement = "robust"` in `compare_null_models()`) flagged under 3% false
interactions, but detected only 15% of the interactions that no mechanism
explains: too strict to detect interactions, but a label for those that do
not depend on the null model.

The script, the rates of every scenario and the report of the simulation are
installed with the package, so that the table can be checked and the
simulation rerun or extended to other designs, effect sizes or numbers of
units:

```{r robustness-files}
dir(system.file("simulations", package = "must"))
```

`source(system.file("simulations", "null_model_robustness.R", package = "must"))`
repeats it with 100 experiments per scenario in about 45 minutes on two cores
(`CORES <- 2` before sourcing it; parallel runs need a Unix-alike) and about
1.5 hours on one.

## Models fitted outside must

`estimate_interactions()` also takes a model fitted with another package
(`lm()`, `glm()`, `mgcv::gam()`, `lme4::glmer()`, `glmmTMB::glmmTMB()` and
the other models supported by emmeans) together with the design of its
data. The contrast sets, null models and tests are the same; the means of
the treatment combinations are the estimated marginal means of emmeans
(random effects at zero, other predictors averaged over), so the stressor,
time and `by` columns of the design must be predictors of the model. For the
small experiment above, the AD interaction of `lm()` is its interaction
coefficient, with the same t interval:

```{r external-lm, eval = has_emmeans}
lm_est <- estimate_interactions(reference, small_design, null_models = c("AD", "MU", "BL"),
                                inference = "delta")
lm_est$estimates[lm_est$estimates$component == "interaction",
                 c("null_model", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "df", "p_value")]
```

Three things are left to the model and to the user. The model is used as
fitted, without the selection of `fit_responses()` or its REML refit; a
combination with only zeros has no usable standard error in such models and
its contrasts are `not_estimable`; and the degrees of freedom are those that
emmeans gives, which are infinite for most generalized and mixed models. With
few experimental units, give them in `df`: here 24 mesocosms in 8 treatment
combinations leave 16.

```{r external-glmmtmb, eval = has_emmeans}
zoo_model <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(
  total_density ~ insecticide * herbicide * nutrients * factor(day) + (1 | mesocosm),
  family = Gamma(link = "log"), data = zoo
)
zoo_est <- estimate_interactions(zoo_model, design, null_models = "MU", n_sim = 4000,
                                 seed = 2021, df = 16)
z <- zoo_est$estimates
z[z$time == "7" & z$order == 3L & z$component == "interaction",
  c("estimand", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "df", "p_adjusted")]
```

The estimates are close to those of the model selected by `fit_responses()`
for this response (a Gamma model with a log link; `triple` above), and the
intervals narrower, because the covariance comes from the maximum-likelihood
fit rather than from the REML refit.

## Decisions and their arguments

| Decision | Argument | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Level that means "no stressor" | `control` in `describe_design()` | none (required) |
| Experimental unit | `unit` | each row |
| Pre-treatment samplings, for all stressors or for each | `baseline` | none |
| Rows shared by every group of a `by` column | `shared` | none |
| Groups of units (blocks, whole plots, rooms) | `groups` | none |
| Other stressors in each interaction | `background` | at control |
| Candidate error distributions | `families`, `response_types` | chosen from the values of each response |
| Successes out of a number of trials | `trials` | none |
| Sampling effort | `offset` | none |
| One dispersion for all, per `by` group or per combination | `dispersion` | `"common"` |
| Treatment effects constant over time? | `time_structure` | `"interaction"` (not constant) |
| Random effects | `random` | intercept per estimable group and per unit when units repeat; removed if its variance is estimated at zero |
| Optimiser limits | `control` | 20 iterations and 30 evaluations per fixed effect |
| Residual checks in the selection | `residual_checks` | `TRUE` (needs DHARMa) |
| Null models | `null_models` | AD (MU, DO, BL, SAM and CA on request, or from `suggest_null_models()`) |
| What is known about the stressors | `similar_action`, `specific_action`, `mortality`, `stressor_effect`, `sensitivity_distribution`, `correlation` in `suggest_null_models()` | unknown: every value is tried |
| Effects of the stressors alone | `effects` in `suggest_null_models()` | estimated from the fitted model |
| Effect close to the effect limit | `near_limit` | 0.9 of the limit |
| Intervals of those effects | `level` in `suggest_null_models()` | 95% |
| Equivalence margin | `margin` | none (no test of equivalence) |
| Shape of the stress capacity in SAM | `sam_shape` | 3.2 (Liess et al. 2016) |
| Uncertainty | `inference`, `n_sim` | Krinsky–Robb simulation, 10000 draws |
| Small-sample correction | `correction` | REML and t distribution |
| Degrees of freedom of a model fitted outside must | `df` | those of emmeans |
| Responses where more means worse | `sensitivity` | none |
| Averages over times | `overall` | `TRUE` |
| Multiple testing | `p_adjust` | Benjamini–Hochberg |
| Random numbers | `seed` | drawn and stored in `settings$seed` |
| Why these null models | `justification` in `report_interactions()` | the criteria of `suggest_null_models()`, or none |

## What a class means

`classify_interactions()` follows Table 1 of Piggott et al. (2015) under AD,
MU, BL, SAM and CA. For three or more stressors the same rules are applied
to the net deviation and its k single effects, a generalization made by this
package. "AD" means that no deviation was detected, not that additivity was
shown; under the other null models, synergism and antagonism are relative to
their own expectation. `borderline = TRUE` marks classes whose adjusted p-values are
so close to `alpha` that another seed could change them. MU and DO only
represent their mechanistic assumptions when an increase in the response
means tolerance (survival, abundance), and AD can predict impossible
negative values (flagged as `expected_below_zero`), in which case a deviation
from it says little about the mechanism (Madge Pimentel et al. 2025).
